newsitem.title: UK: Gold falls, base metals mute gains, wheat is firm.
newsitem.headline: Gold falls, base metals mute gains, wheat is firm.

text.p: A volatile week in world commodity markets ended with gold looking sickly and grains and the key industrial metals not sure whether to extend their rallies.

But oil prices again headed upward on fears that heating oil may be tight in the northern winter. Gold had slumped on Thursday to its lowest in almost two years at $375.70 per ounce. It closed London on Friday at $377.15 and eased again in New York activity.
The bullion market has before it the latest views from one of the leading metals analysts, Ted Arnold at Merrill Lynch, who sees gold dropping to $350 at some point in 1997.

Arnold expects producers of gold to make forward sales in to any rally. A cap of that kind may continue to discourage the speculators who have sold gold in recent days. Arnold also saw copper as bearish in 1997 despite a recent brisk rally above $2,200 per tonne, up from $1,745 hit during the Sumitomo scandal in mid-June. He expected "reasonably high copper prices" for a few months but said that fundamentals of supply and demand were bearish from the second half of 1997 onwards.

Copper ended Friday in London dipping from a high of $2,218 per tonne to settle at $2,208, down $4 on the day. It eased further in late inter-office activity. Copper has rallied lately on news that supervised warehouse stocks are at six-year lows.
Aluminium reached a 3-1/2 month high of $1,535 a tonne in a tight physical market that attracted investment fund buying on Friday.
Benchmark Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) wheat futures were again firm, just above $4.00 per bushel on signs of a tighter U.S. market and despite a profit-taking sell-off on Thursday.
Oil prices rallied on Friday to wipe out midweek losses as much of the United States remained in the icy grip of an early winter, prompting fears of heating oil shortages.
January futures for the benchmark North Sea Brent Blend of crude oil were more than 30 cents firmer late in London's day at almost $23.40 a barrel.

Jon Davies, Chicago-based meteorologist at brokers Smith Barney, on Friday forecast temperatures would be six to 12 degrees below normal from the U.S. Rocky Mountain region to the East Coast until the end of the month.
Oil ministers of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) meet in Vienna next week but are unlikely to raise supply quotas.
